items.title: E1. Exact block accounting
items.prompt: Compute the matrix-only and full counts for the Llama-3.1-8B block.
items.answer:
*Solution.* In GQA, $Q$ and $O$ are $d\times d$, while K/V width is one quarter of $d$. The two K/V matrices therefore contribute $2d(d/4)=0.5d^2$, giving

$$P_{attn}=2d^2+0.5d^2=2.5d^2.$$

SwiGLU has gate, up, and down projections. With $d_{ff}=3.5d$, their count is $3dd_{ff}=10.5d^2$. Thus

$$P_{matrix}=13d^2=13\cdot4096^2=218{,}103{,}808.$$

Two RMSNorm scales add $2d=8192$, yielding **218,112,000**. Biases are excluded by this architecture contract.

items.title: E2. Epsilon and gain
items.prompt: Compare the RMSNorm multipliers at input RMS $10^{-3}$ for $\epsilon=10^{-6}$ and $10^{-5}$.
items.answer:
*Solution.* RMSNorm divides by $\sqrt{\operatorname{RMS}(x)^2+\epsilon}$. Here the signal-square term is $10^{-6}$, so

$$g_{10^{-6}}=1/\sqrt{2\cdot10^{-6}}\approx707.1,$$
$$g_{10^{-5}}=1/\sqrt{11\cdot10^{-6}}\approx301.5.$$

The larger epsilon more than halves the gain because it dominates this small signal. Epsilon must therefore reflect reduction precision and expected activation scale, not dtype machine epsilon alone.

items.title: E3. The negative gpt-oss branch
items.prompt: Explain why the up-branch clip still changes the $z=-9$ case.
items.answer:
*Solution.* Use $g=\min(z,7)$, $u=\operatorname{clip}(z,-7,7)$, and $y=g\sigma(1.702g)(u+1)$:

| $z$ | $g$ | $u$ | $y$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| -9 | -9 | -7 | 0.000012019 |
| -2 | -2 | -2 | 0.064341377 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 5.806975869 |
| 7 | 7 | 7 | 55.999625026 |
| 9 | 7 | 7 | 55.999625026 |

At $z=-9$, the gate is not lower-clipped and its sigmoid nearly suppresses it, but the up branch is still changed to $-7$ and enters as $u+1=-6$. The output is small because of the gate, not because the clip is irrelevant. At 7 and 9, both used branches are identical, so the outputs match.

items.title: E6. Scaling and reduction axes
items.prompt: Why does fixed positive epsilon break exact scale invariance? How does changing one head affect per-head and whole-projection RMSNorm?
items.answer:
*Solution.* For a positive scale $c$, factor it out of the denominator:

$$
\frac{cx}{\sqrt{c^2\operatorname{mean}(x^2)+\epsilon}}
=\frac{x}{\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(x^2)+\epsilon/c^2}}.
$$

Keeping $\epsilon>0$ fixed therefore changes the normalization. With a single value $x=10^{-3}$, $\epsilon=10^{-6}$, and unit learned scale, the output is $1/\sqrt2\approx0.7071$. Doubling the input gives $2/\sqrt5\approx0.8944$. The stabilizer is comparable to the squared signal, so the difference is substantial.

When RMS is reduced over all heads together, scaling one head changes the shared denominator and hence the untouched heads too. Separate head-wise reductions keep their denominators independent. Predict which heads will change before comparing the two notebook calculations.

items.title: E7. Doubly stochastic does not mean identity
items.prompt: Verify the example in §12. Does satisfying both sum constraints imply $AX=X$?
items.answer:
*Solution.* Each row and column of the matrix in §12 sums to $0.75+0.25=1$. Its first output is $0.75\cdot2+0.25\cdot6=3$; its second is $0.25\cdot2+0.75\cdot6=5$. Thus $AX=(3,5)^\top\ne X$.

Nonnegative entries and unit row sums make each output a convex combination, bounded between 2 and 6. The output range can shrink: here it is 3 to 5. Unit column sums additionally preserve the sum across streams: $3+5=2+6$. Neither property preserves each stream separately. After a finite number of Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations, check both sum residuals before treating these properties as exact.
